voice_event.text:
To us, Jesus is the Only-Begotten of God - the Ihidaya, our own name for him. He left his place with God and made his home in the Virgin, and by being born as we are born, he became the brother of many. In him the words of the prophets, kings, and priests came true - the Nativity hymns sing of the day that made them glad, because every old promise came true at Bethlehem. His death and rising are one rescue. He went down into Sheol, the world of the dead that swallows everyone alike, and came out into the Kingdom. His own resurrection is the promise that he will bring us out after him. And what it meant to those who followed him was healing: he is the Physician, and his coming is medicine for a wounded people.

Our own poet put it this way: "The Only-Begotten left his place with God. He made his home in the Virgin. He took a body from her and put it on. He came out into creation as a small child".

glosses.plain_meaning: The Single One. One word does double duty among us. It names the vowed celibate - single-minded, undivided for God - and it is also the Syriac title of Christ as the Only-Begotten. The two senses share one root: to live single is to be joined, by your own name, to Christ's own oneness.
glosses.quick_meaning: The Single One: our word for the vowed celibate - and, at the same time, our title for Christ the Only-Begotten.
glosses.translational_sense: 'Solitary' misleads: the ihidaye lived among the congregation, not in isolation; the singleness is of heart and allegiance, not of address.

voice_event.text:
He healed. That is the first answer, and the one we returned to most often. Our teachers preached him as the Physician who came for the wounded, and a physician exists for wounds, not in spite of them. He received the one who came to him in tears, past every watching eye - we told that story again and again, because in her we saw the door standing open. And he went into death's own country and broke it. Our hymns stage Death himself trembling, complaining that Jesus had plundered his house. He took sin and nailed it to his cross. His rising became the pledge that Sheol gives back its dead.

What he did not do: he did not leave the wounded to hide their wounds. He did not come only for the ones who had it right already. And he did not promise exemption from the blow - his own answer to suffering was presence and resurrection after, not rescue before it lands.

voice_event.text:
The Single One. One word does double duty among us. It names the vowed celibate - single-minded, undivided for God - and it is also the Syriac title of Christ as the Only-Begotten. The two senses share one root: to live single is to be joined, by your own name, to Christ's own oneness.

The men and women who took the covenant - the qyama - and vowed their whole lives to celibacy and service, staying in town among their own kin rather than leaving for the desert, were called ihidaye, the single ones. They carried that name because their life was undivided, given wholly to God. And at the same time, Ihidaya was our own title for Jesus himself, the Only-Begotten. The two meanings were never rivals. To be called an ihidaya was to wear Christ's own name as your own.

glosses.plain_meaning: The covenant: our own vowed order. Its members - the sons and daughters of the covenant - promised a celibate life for good. But they did not leave for the desert. They stayed in town, among their own kin, and served the congregation: the fast, the watch, the vigil, the singing.
glosses.quick_meaning: The covenant: our vowed order of celibate men and women. They stayed in town and served the congregation, rather than leave for the desert.
glosses.translational_sense: 'Were they monks and nuns?' - no monastery, no desert, no later rule: a vow taken for life, lived at home, in the congregation's daily service.
false_friend: monk or nun (desert withdrawal, cloister, formal rule)

We believed Jesus is the Only-Begotten who dwelt in the Virgin and broke death's rule because we received it as witness, tested it in how people lived, and sang it until the truth was woven into our bones. The Gospel we read in worship - the one continuous story Tatian had woven from the four accounts - gave us the narrative whole. The prophets, kings, and priests had all spoken of him, and at Bethlehem every old promise came true. That was the ground we stood on: Scripture pointing to him, and the resurrection as the pledge that Sheol gives back its dead.

And we believed it against neighbors who taught otherwise. Marcion said the Maker of this world was not the Father of Jesus - we said he was. Bardaisan said God worked with eternal elements - we said God made all things from nothing. Mani split the world between two powers - we refused it. Knowing what we believed meant answering, by name, what we did not. On the Persian side, people died for this confession under a hostile crown. That was the other test: not argument alone, but what it cost to hold it.
